description: We are Team Psycodes, students from DIU, BRAC University and Jahangirnagar University, Bangladesh. We're building Atmos X, an app that uses NASA satellite data to find the hottest city blocks, plan tree planting to cool them, and give farmers early weather alerts. Our skills: UI design, Next.js front end, FastAPI back end, DevOps and QA. We're looking for teammates skilled in remote sensing, satellite data or climate science. Join us!
summary:
Atmos-X is a heat and weather-risk platform for Bangladesh that turns NASA open data into action for two groups who feel the heat first: city residents and farmers. Some streets run far hotter than others, and farmers often get no warning before heat, flash floods or drought hit their crops at harvest.

Atmos-X does three things. See the heat: it maps heat street by street and shows why a block is hot, with a heat score, surface versus air temperature, sealed ground and green cover. Plan the cooling: it builds a costed cooling plan (trees, cool roofs) with the expected temperature drop. Prove it works: it tracks the change over time with the same satellite data. For farmers, it sends field alerts up to 48 hours ahead, such as heat at flowering, flash-flood risk after heavy rain, or a dry spell, with a clear action like harvesting the ripe rows first.

Atmos-X combines 15 NASA datasets, including live satellite data, and Atmos AI lets anyone ask questions in plain language. Cooler cities, safer harvests and more trees connect seven UN Sustainable Development Goals in one loop.
details:
What it does

NASA already measures street-level heat, rain and air quality, but communities and farmers cannot turn that data into local action. Atmos X closes that gap with one loop from scan to proof:

1. Scan: pick a radius from 100 m to 1 km, split into H3 hexagon zones.

2. See: the hottest zones, each with a Heat Score and its causes (concrete, low greenery, density), today's BMD heat-wave level versus the 30-year normal, a 5-day NASA forecast, and a time slider of surface heat back to 2000.

3. Set a goal: a °C target and date, checked for feasibility.

4. Plan: a costed action plan of trees, cool roofs, shade and water, with quantities, species, cost, an itemized budget split and cost per °C of cooling. An empty-space finder locates open land and roofs, and a "with vs without" chart shows what the plan changes over time.

5. Act: alone, in a team of 2 to 5, or as a school, NGO or city body, with a nursery map for saplings.

6. Verify: each action is logged with GPS and time, AI checks the photo matches the spot, and tree check-ins track survival. Progress is measured against nearby untouched control zones, so a hotter year does not read as failure.

Community, points and leaderboards

Cooling a neighborhood works best together, so Atmos X is built for community action:

- Act alone, in a team of 2 to 5, or as a school, NGO or city body, and share one goal and plan.

- Every action earns points: plant a tree, paint a cool roof, add shade or water. Each action is logged with GPS and time, and AI checks that the photo matches the spot, so points reflect real work.

- Badges and levels mark progress, and community leaderboards rank people and groups by area and by country, so neighborhoods and schools can compete to cool their streets.

- Tree care keeps it going: public and personal trees get check-ins twice a month to track survival.

Farmer mode, air and Ask Atmos

Farmer mode sends eight alerts up to 48 hours ahead: flash flood, heat at flowering, drought, cyclone harvest, cold wave, late blight, monsoon onset and lightning. Air quality (PM2.5 and AQI) blends stations, sensors and NASA GEOS-CF. Ask Atmos, an AI chat on every screen, answers from Atmos X data, shows official bulletins first and never acts without a tap to confirm.

Benefits and intended impact

Atmos X turns satellite archives into a first step people can take this week: which block to cool, what to plant, what it costs and whether it worked. Points and leaderboards keep neighborhoods coming back, and verified photos keep the results honest. Farmers get warnings before heat, floods or drought hit at flowering or harvest. Cooler streets, safer harvests and more surviving trees connect seven UN Sustainable Development Goals in one loop, starting with Dhaka and designed to grow to more cities.

Tools, languages and software

- Frontend: Next.js installable web app (PWA), React and TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre and deck.gl, next-intl in 10 languages including Bangla and English.

- Backend: NestJS API, Prisma ORM, Redis and BullMQ jobs, Web Push and email.

- Data: PostgreSQL with PostGIS and h3-pg hexagons, S3-compatible storage.

- Science worker: Python with FastAPI, Google Earth Engine, earthaccess and the AppEEARS API, pulling and processing NASA data on a schedule.

NASA data: Landsat 8 and 9 surface temperature, HLS v2.0, MODIS MOD11A1 and MAIAC aerosol, ECOSTRESS LST, NASA POWER, GEOS-FP, GEOS-CF, SEDAC GMIS and GPW v4, GPM IMERG, SMAP L4 soil moisture, LIS/OTD lightning climatology and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, accessed through Earthdata, CMR-STAC, AppEEARS and GIBS.

Other sources, always labeled as non-NASA in the app: Open-Meteo, OpenAQ, Sensor. Community, PurpleAir, ESA WorldCover, Google Dynamic World, Google Open Buildings and OpenStreetMap.


Community, points and leaderboards Cooling a neighbourhood works best together, so Atmos X is built for community action:

- Act alone, in a team of 2 to 5, or as a school, NGO or city body, and share one goal and plan.

- Every action earns points: plant a tree, paint a cool roof, add shade or water. Each action is logged with GPS and time, and AI checks that the photo matches the spot, so points reflect real work.

- Badges and levels mark progress, and community leaderboards rank people and groups by area and by country, so neighborhoods and schools can compete to cool their streets.

- Tree care keeps it going: public and personal trees get check-ins twice a month to track survival, and members earn points for keeping them alive.


How it is creative

Atmos X does not stop at a heat map. It closes the loop from data to action to proof, uses control zones to judge results fairly, and turns cooling into a shared game with verified points, badges and community leaderboards. The same NASA data serves city residents and farmers in one app.

Factors we considered

- Fairness: results are compared with untouched zones, so a hot year does not erase real progress.

- Honesty: non-NASA data is labeled, AI-checked photos stop fake points, empty spaces are candidates the user confirms on the ground, and official bulletins come first.

- Privacy: a user's own air sensor stays private for 7 days.

- Access: 10 languages, °C or °F, an installable app; next we plan SMS and voice alerts for basic phones.

- Coverage: TEMPO only covers North America, so for Dhaka we use GEOS-CF plus MODIS aerosol for air.
